summary: A collection of poems presented at Act One, a symposium held partly to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the ARPANET. It is a lighthearted informational document.

eli5.summary: This is a small book of poems read at a party for the Internet's twentieth birthday.

subtitle: A collection of poems celebrating the 20th anniversary of the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: The early days of packet switching and computer networking were momentous but largely documented only in technical terms.
tldr.mechanism: At a 1989 symposium at UCLA marking the ARPANET's 20th anniversary, speakers including Leonard Kleinrock, Vint Cerf, and Barry Boehm presented poems reflecting on the network's history and future.
tldr.outcome: This RFC preserves five poems that capture the spirit of the Internet's pioneers and their vision for networking technology, written from the perspective of people who were there at the beginning.

today: RFC 1121 is an informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains a unique record of how the Internet's pioneers reflected on their work and celebrated a milestone in computing history.

sections.title: The Symposium and the Poems
sections.content:
RFC 1121 is a collection of five poems presented at "Act One," a symposium held by UCLA's Computer Science Department on August 17-18, 1989, to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the ARPANET. The first Interface Message Processor (IMP) had been installed at UCLA in 1969, making the university the first node on the network.

The poets were all significant figures in networking history: Leonard Kleinrock, who had led the symposium, Vint Cerf (co-inventor of TCP), and Barry Boehm. The poems range from historical narratives to playful parodies, capturing the pioneering spirit of the era.
sections.eli5: This document contains poems written by the inventors of the Internet, read at a party in 1989 to remember how it all started in 1969.

sections.title: The Five Poems
sections.content:
Kleinrock wrote four poems: "Welcome," an opening address; "Ode to a Queue," celebrating the mathematics of queuing theory that underlies network modeling; "The Past is Prologue," a brief reflection on the transition from past to future; and "The Big Bang!," a humorous narrative in rhyming couplets about the chaotic arrival and setup of the first IMP at UCLA.

Cerf's "Rosencrantz and Ethernet" is a parody of Shakespeare's Hamlet, replacing existential questions about life with questions about switching vs. packet routing. Boehm's untitled poem is a five-stanza humorous verse about Paul Baran, DARPA funding, network technology, and Leonard Kleinrock's continued expertise.
sections.eli5: Kleinrock wrote funny verses about building networks and queues (waiting lines). Cerf made jokes using Shakespeare. Boehm wrote about the invention of the network and praised Kleinrock's knowledge.

sections.title: Themes and History
sections.content:
The poems emphasize the historical moment of the ARPANET's creation in 1967-1969, the technical challenges that were overcome, and the personalities involved. "The Big Bang!" vividly depicts the arrival of the first IMP at UCLA: "But one day after Labor Day, it was plopped down at our gate! Those dirty rotten scoundrels sent the damned thing out air freight!"

They celebrate DARPA's funding of research, the analytical methods that shaped network design, and the engineers and researchers who made it work. The poems also hint at future directions: Kleinrock's reference to "high speed nets on Friday" and Boehm's mention of diverse network types (VAN's, MAN's, WAN's) suggest the developers' vision of a rich networking ecosystem beyond the ARPANET itself.
sections.eli5: The poems tell the true story of how the first network computer showed up by airplane and how surprised everyone was that it actually worked.

sections.title: Legacy and Significance
sections.content:
RFC 1121 preserves a unique moment in computing history, when the ARPANET's pioneers gathered to reflect on what they had built and imagine its future. The poems capture the blend of technical achievement, humor, and camaraderie that characterized the early Internet community.

As the only RFC consisting entirely of creative writing about computing, it stands out in the technical literature as a record of how engineers expressed themselves about their work when formal standards were not required.
sections.eli5: This document is special because it shows the inventors of the Internet being creative and funny about their work, something you don't usually see in rule books.
